intro: Real archaeological finds tied to each Deep Dive period — house churches, inscriptions, catacombs, basilicas, and everyday Christian things. Evidence shows, scholars infer, and still debated stay separate. Photo credits sit under each image.

context.title: The world of the Gospels
context.note: Jewish and Roman finds that set the scene for the Gospels. These are not Christian artifacts.

items.name: Caiaphas family ossuary
items.date_note: Inscribed “Joseph son of Caiaphas”; identification with the high priest is widely accepted but not certain.
items.now: Israel Museum, Jerusalem
items.line: A limestone bone box inscribed with a name matching the high-priestly family in the Gospels. It belongs to Jewish burial practice of the Second Temple period.

evidence.shows: A Jerusalem ossuary of the period bears the name Joseph son of Caiaphas.
evidence.infer: Likely the high priest Joseph Caiaphas known from Josephus and the New Testament.
evidence.debated: Whether this exact box held the high priest himself (vs. a relative of the same name).

items.connect_why: Places Gospel-era Jerusalem priesthood in the material world of names and burial customs.

items.name: Pilate Stone (Caesarea inscription)
items.date_note: Date of the dedication is within Pilate’s term; the block was reused later in Caesarea’s theater.
items.now: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (copy often displayed at Caesarea)
items.line: A Latin building dedication naming “[Pon]tius Pilatus, Prefect of Judea.” It is independent Roman evidence for the prefect named in the Gospels.

evidence.shows: A Roman official named Pontius Pilatus held the title prefect of Judea and dedicated a Tiberieum at Caesarea.
evidence.infer: Usual reconstruction of the damaged lines; that this is the same Pilate as in the passion narratives.
evidence.debated: Exact wording of some restored letters; the stone is not a Christian artifact.

items.connect_why: Gives solid Roman-world footing for the prefect named in the passion accounts and later Roman notices.

items.name: Pool of Siloam
items.date: Second Temple period pool; stepped pool excavated 2004 onward
items.date_note: The large stepped pool south of the Temple Mount is widely identified with the Siloam pool of John 9; work and interpretation continue.
items.now: In situ (archaeological park area)
items.line: A large stepped pool fed by the Gihon spring via Hezekiah’s Tunnel. John’s Gospel places a healing of a blind man here.

evidence.shows: A monumental Second Temple–period pool exists at the traditional Siloam location.
evidence.infer: This is the pool known to first-century Jerusalem and to the Johannine narrative setting.
evidence.debated: Full extent and phases of the complex; how visitors should picture the Gospel scene.

items.connect_why: Grounds Gospel and early-Jerusalem geography in a real water system people still walk today.

items.name: Capernaum “House of Peter”
items.date: 1st-century house remains; Christian meeting use by ~late 1st–4th c.; octagonal memorial church later
items.date_note: Identification with Peter’s house is traditional and debated; archaeology shows a house later treated as sacred.
items.found: Capernaum (Kfar Nahum), Sea of Galilee, Israel
items.now: Under the modern memorial church; Franciscan Custody / IAA oversight of excavations
items.line: Excavators found a first-century house whose main room was later plastered, inscribed, and set apart, then covered by an octagonal church. Pilgrims remembered it as Peter’s home.

evidence.shows: A Capernaum house was adapted for Christian gathering and later monumentalized.
evidence.infer: Early local memory linked the house to Peter and to Jesus’ Capernaum ministry.
evidence.debated: Whether the house actually belonged to Peter; how early the Christian use began.

items.connect_why: Puts Peter’s Galilean world and later Christian memory of place side by side with the earliest narrative texts.
items.caution: Tradition links this house to Peter; archaeology shows a house later treated as sacred, but the identification with Peter himself is debated.

items.name: Rotas–Sator square (Pompeii)
items.date_note: Christian reading (Pater Noster cross, etc.) is heavily debated; the square also appears in later clearly Christian contexts.
items.now: In situ / Pompeii archaeological site documentation; casts and photos widely published
items.line: A five-word Latin palindrome square (ROTAS OPERA TENET AREPO SATOR). Some read a hidden Christian prayer; others see a pagan word-play or magic square.

evidence.shows: The square existed in the Vesuvian cities before 79.
evidence.infer: Possible early Christian presence — or none.
evidence.debated: Whether the Pompeii squares are Christian at all.

items.connect_why: If Christian, it would be startlingly early Italian evidence; if not, it still shows why caution labels matter.
items.caution: The square is real and early; whether it is Christian at all is still debated.

items.name: Rylands Papyrus P52 (John)
items.date: Often placed early–mid 2nd century; some scholars prefer later 2nd / ~200
items.date_note: Palaeographic dating only; no secure archaeological find-spot date.
items.found: Egypt (acquired early 20th c.; exact find-spot uncertain)
items.now: John Rylands Library, University of Manchester
items.line: A tiny scrap of a papyrus codex with John 18 on both sides. It is among the earliest surviving pieces of any New Testament book.

evidence.shows: A Greek copy of John’s Gospel circulated in Egypt in a codex format by roughly the 2nd century.
evidence.infer: How early John was composed and how fast it spread; that Christians preferred the codex early.
evidence.debated: Exact date within the 2nd century (or slightly later).

items.connect_why: Physical remnant of the Gospel texts early Christians were already quoting and circulating.

items.name: Alexamenos graffito
items.date_note: Dating from context of the Palatine paedagogium; exact year unknown.
items.now: Palatine Museum, Rome
items.line: A scratched cartoon of a person raising a hand toward a crucified figure with a donkey’s head, with Greek words mocking “Alexamenos” for worshipping his god. One of the earliest pictures of a crucifixion scene.

evidence.shows: Someone in Rome mocked a person named Alexamenos for worshipping a crucified god.
evidence.infer: The mocked figure is Jesus; the joke reflects pagan contempt for the cross.
evidence.debated: Exact date; whether the donkey-head is a specific anti-Jewish/anti-Christian slur tradition.

items.connect_why: Matches the tone of pagan mockery the apologists answer when they defend the crucified Christ.

items.name: Bodmer papyri (incl. P75 / Hanna Papyrus)
items.date: Roughly late 2nd–early 3rd century for key NT leaves (debated)
items.date_note: P75 (Luke/John) now in the Vatican Library as Hanna Papyrus 1.
items.now: Bodmer Foundation, Cologny; Vatican Apostolic Library (P75)
items.line: Early, carefully written Gospel papyri. P75 is famous for its close kinship to later great parchment Bibles.

evidence.shows: High-quality Gospel copies existed in Egypt before Constantine’s parchment pandects.
evidence.infer: Pathways from early papyri to Codex Vaticanus-type text.
evidence.debated: Precise dates; relationship details between P75 and Vaticanus.

items.connect_why: Bridges the world of Origen to the great 4th-century Bibles.

items.name: Catacomb of Domitilla (arcosolium)
items.date_note: One of Rome’s largest Christian catacombs; individual paintings vary in date.
items.now: In situ; open to visitors under Pontifical Commission / site management
items.line: Vast underground galleries and painted arcosolia. Domitilla preserves the scale of Christian burial networks under Rome before and after Constantine.

evidence.shows: Large organized Christian cemeteries existed beneath Rome.
evidence.infer: Links to Flavian-era Christian households in tradition; growth patterns of the community.
evidence.debated: Which earliest nuclei are securely Christian vs. mixed.

items.connect_why: Makes “the church in Rome” feel like tunnels, names, and painted tombs — not an abstraction.

items.name: Chester Beatty biblical papyri
items.date_note: Includes early Pauline and Gospels codices (e.g. P45, P46, P47).
items.found: Egypt (exact find circumstances partly obscure; acquired 1930s)
items.now: Chester Beatty Library, Dublin
items.line: A group of early papyrus codices of Scripture — Gospels, Paul, Revelation — showing how third-century Christians copied and carried their books.

evidence.shows: Substantial New Testament texts circulated in codex form in 3rd-century Egypt.
evidence.infer: Scribal habits, early canon clusters, and textual variants.
evidence.debated: Exact find-spot history for some lots.

items.connect_why: Origen’s Egypt is suddenly full of real Bible pages you can photograph.

items.name: Chi-Rho oil lamp (Met)
items.date_note: Wide date range; symbol is Christian chi-rho on a household lamp from Egypt.
items.now: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (17.194.1813) — Public Domain / CC0 image policy
items.line: A small clay lamp stamped with the chi-rho. Someone lit their evening room with Christ’s monogram — faith in the furniture of ordinary life.

evidence.shows: Christian symbols appeared on mass-produced household lamps.
evidence.infer: Protective and identity use of the christogram in daily settings.
evidence.debated: Where within the long date range any one lamp falls.

items.connect_why: After the chi-rho enters imperial story under Constantine, you can also hold it as a cheap clay light.

items.name: Christ-Helios mosaic (Tomb of the Julii)
items.date_note: Mausoleum M under St Peter’s; Christian reading of solar Christ is standard but the blend with Sol imagery is striking.
items.found: Vatican Necropolis (scavi), under St Peter’s Basilica
items.now: In situ (scavi); access by Vatican guided tour
items.line: A ceiling mosaic of a chariot-riding figure with a rayed nimbus among vines — widely read as Christ using the visual language of Sol Invictus.

evidence.shows: A Vatican necropolis tomb mixed Christian and solar imagery before or around Constantine’s time.
evidence.infer: Christ as true “sun” of salvation; deliberate reuse of imperial solar art.
evidence.debated: Exact date; how consciously “anti-Sol” vs. simply shared artistic vocabulary.

items.connect_why: Shows Christians speaking in the visual dialect of the late Roman world just as the empire turns.

items.name: Dura-Europos house church & baptistery
items.date: Converted ~AD 232–256 (city fell to the Sasanians c. 256)
items.date_note: Yale dates baptistery paintings ca. 232–245; building history refined in ongoing scholarship.
items.now: Wall paintings at Yale University Art Gallery (CC0); site in Syria
items.line: The earliest securely dated Christian house church. A domestic building was adapted with a meeting hall and a painted baptistery (Good Shepherd, healing scenes, women at the tomb).

evidence.shows: Third-century Christians at Dura baptized in a decorated room and met in a remodeled house.
evidence.infer: How typical this arrangement was; exact reading of some painted scenes.
evidence.debated: Degree of “church” vs. continuing domestic use; some iconographic identifications.

items.connect_why: Reading On Baptism or Justin’s worship description, you can look at an actual baptistery from the same century.

items.name: Fractio Panis (breaking of the bread) — Priscilla
items.date_note: Dating varies by scholar; the scene is among the earliest banquet/Eucharist images.
items.found: Greek Chapel, Catacomb of Priscilla, Rome
items.now: In situ; Pontifical Commission for Sacred Archaeology
items.line: A banquet scene with a figure breaking bread at a table — long read as an early image of the Eucharist or agape meal.

evidence.shows: Christians painted communal meal imagery in a Roman catacomb chapel.
evidence.infer: Eucharistic meaning (fractio panis); some see a funerary banquet more broadly.
evidence.debated: How specifically “Mass-like” vs. funerary meal the scene is.

items.connect_why: Paul and Justin describe a shared loaf; here is a loaf being broken on a wall.

image.alt: Fractio Panis (breaking of the bread) — Priscilla

items.name: Good Shepherd fresco (Catacomb of Priscilla)
items.date_note: Catacomb painting chronology is approximate.
items.now: In situ; under Pontifical Commission for Sacred Archaeology
items.line: Christ as a young shepherd carrying a sheep — tender, everyday imagery in a burial place. Among the best-known early Christian paintings.

evidence.shows: Roman Christians used shepherd imagery in funerary art well before Constantine.
evidence.infer: Link to John 10 / Luke 15 and to pagan shepherd motifs reused for Christ.
evidence.debated: Exact chapel date within the catacomb’s long use.

items.connect_why: The Shepherd of Hermas and Gospel shepherd language meet a picture on a tomb wall.

items.name: Good Shepherd — Catacomb of Callixtus (Lucina)
items.date_note: Published in Wilpert’s early-20th-century plates; site managed by the Pontifical Commission.
items.now: In situ; Pontifical Commission for Sacred Archaeology
items.line: Another early Good Shepherd in the papal cemetery of Callixtus — the same image language as Priscilla, in the burial ground of many early popes and martyrs.

evidence.shows: Shepherd Christ imagery was shared across major Roman Christian cemeteries.
evidence.infer: Continuity of hope-for-the-dead imagery before public basilicas.
evidence.debated: Fine-grained dating of individual cubicula.

items.connect_why: Callixtus is the cemetery named in third-century Roman church conflicts Deep Dive already covers.

items.name: Inscription of Abercius
items.date_note: Partly known from a later copy dated 216 (Alexander of Hierapolis); original fragments recovered 1883.
items.found: Hieropolis (Hierapolis area), Phrygia, Turkey — reused in a bath building
items.now: Vatican Museums, Museo Pio Cristiano
items.line: A Greek verse epitaph in coded Christian language: a “holy Shepherd,” travel to Rome, “pure fish,” bread and wine. The Vatican calls it the most ancient known Christian inscription.

evidence.shows: A late-2nd/early-3rd-century Phrygian Christian used cryptic Eucharistic and ecclesial imagery on his tomb.
evidence.infer: Abercius was a bishop of Hierapolis; the “queen” is the Roman church.
evidence.debated: How much of the later Life of Abercius can be trusted beyond the stone.

items.connect_why: Deep Dive already includes the text; the stone is the thing itself in the Vatican.

items.name: Livia Primitiva funerary slab (fish & anchor)
items.date_note: Classic example of fish + anchor Christian funerary symbols.
items.found: Rome (catacomb context; now in museum collections — Louvre often cited for the plaque)
items.now: Musée du Louvre, Paris (commonly referenced)
items.line: A simple tomb slab with fish and an anchor — quiet symbols of hope and of Christ the fish (ICHTHYS) that ordinary believers could carve without a long inscription.

evidence.shows: Fish and anchor were used as Christian funerary signs in Rome.
evidence.infer: Anchor as hope (Hebrews 6:19); fish as Christ acronym.
evidence.debated: Whether every fish/anchor plaque is certainly Christian (most with clear Christian context are).

items.connect_why: Shows the small symbolic language everyday Christians used alongside the big literary texts.

items.name: Megiddo (Kefar ‘Othnay) prayer hall mosaic
items.date: IAA: 3rd century (often ~AD 230); some scholars argue later 3rd/4th
items.date_note: Date rests on coins, pottery, and paleography; not universally agreed.
items.now: Israel Antiquities Authority; mosaic conserved for display (site relocation/preservation ongoing)
items.line: A mosaic floor with fish and three Greek inscriptions, including a woman Akeptous who “offered the table to God Jesus Christ.” A rare pre-Constantinian worship room.

evidence.shows: A Christian assembly room with a donated “table” and an inscription naming God Jesus Christ.
evidence.infer: Eucharistic use of the table; significant Christian presence among Roman military personnel at Legio.
evidence.debated: Precise date within the 3rd–early 4th century; how “church-like” the building was.

items.connect_why: Lets a reader of Justin or Paul suddenly see a real table dedication and fish mosaic from the same world.

items.name: Orans (praying figure) — Priscilla
items.date_note: Orans figures are common across Roman catacombs.
items.now: In situ; Pontifical Commission for Sacred Archaeology
items.line: A veiled woman with arms raised in prayer — the classic orans posture. A quiet, human glimpse of how early Christians pictured prayer.

evidence.shows: Prayer with raised arms was a valued image in Christian burial art.
evidence.infer: Often read as the soul of the deceased, or the Church at prayer.
evidence.debated: Identity of particular orans figures (portrait vs. type).

items.connect_why: Matches the praying Church described in early letters and visions.

image.credit: Painting, unknown artist, 3rd century A.D., Rome photo by Joseph…

items.name: Pectorius (Autun) inscription
items.date_note: Acrostic ICHTHYS poem; scholarly dating not unanimous.
items.now: Musée Rolin, Autun (commonly cited)
items.line: A Greek epitaph that plays on ICHTHYS (fish) and speaks of the “fish” from the spring, heavenly food, and baptismal washing — poetry thick with Eucharistic and baptismal hints.

evidence.shows: Gallic Christians used Greek fish symbolism in funerary verse.
evidence.infer: Strong sacramental reading of the lines.
evidence.debated: Precise century.

items.connect_why: Pairs beautifully with Abercius: two coded fish/Eucharist inscriptions at opposite ends of the Christian map.

items.name: St Peter’s tomb area (Vatican necropolis / scavi)
items.date: 2nd-century shrine (“Trophy of Gaius”); Constantinian basilica above; excavations 1939–
items.date_note: A 2nd-century memorial on the site is widely accepted; whether particular bones are Peter’s remains debated.
items.found: Under St Peter’s Basilica, Vatican City
items.now: Vatican scavi (guided access)
items.line: Excavations under the high altar revealed a pagan necropolis and a second-century memorial traditionally linked to Peter’s grave, later enclosed by Constantine’s basilica.

evidence.shows: A carefully marked memorial stood on this spot by the 2nd century; Constantine built directly over it.
evidence.infer: Early Roman Christian memory of Peter’s burial here (cf. Gaius in Eusebius).
evidence.debated: Identification of specific bones as Peter’s; reading of some graffiti (“Petros eni”).

items.connect_why: 1 Clement and Eusebius talk about Peter in Rome; the scavi show the place Rome remembered.
items.caution: A second-century memorial on this spot is well established; whether particular bones are Peter’s remains is still debated.

image.alt: St Peter’s tomb area (Vatican necropolis / scavi)

items.name: Aquileia basilica mosaics
items.date_note: UNESCO site; huge mosaic carpets with Jonah, donors, and daily life.
items.now: In situ under the later medieval basilica floor (viewable)
items.line: Ocean-floor mosaics of a 4th-century church: fish, Jonah, portraits of donors — a whole congregation’s floor still under glass.

evidence.shows: Northern Italian Christians paved worship halls with narrative and donor mosaics in the 300s.
evidence.infer: Wealth, patronage, and teaching-through-floor-art.
evidence.debated: Exact sequence of the Theodorian building phases.

items.connect_why: Shows post-Constantinian worship space outside Rome and the Holy Land.

image.credit: No machine-readable author provided. G.dallorto assumed (based on…

items.name: Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem
items.date_note: Present structure is largely Crusader and later; Constantinian plan known from texts and archaeology.
items.now: In use; shared Christian custody
items.line: The complex over Golgotha and the tomb. Whatever one makes of every stone, it is the pilgrimage heart Egeria walked and Cyril explained.

evidence.shows: Constantine’s architects monumentalized a tomb site in 4th-century Jerusalem; worship continues.
evidence.infer: Continuity with pre-Constantinian local memory of the tomb.
evidence.debated: How much of the present fabric maps to the first church; details of the tomb aedicule’s earlier forms.

items.connect_why: Primary Deep Dive pilgrimage and mystagogy texts become places underfoot.

image.alt: Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem

items.name: Church of the Nativity, Bethlehem
items.date: Constantinian foundation 4th c.; major Justinianic rebuild 6th c.
items.date_note: UNESCO World Heritage; still a living church.
items.now: In use; shared custody; UNESCO site
items.line: The cave Christians remembered as Jesus’ birth place, roofed by imperial church architecture. Pilgrims have come for seventeen centuries.

evidence.shows: A continuous church complex stands over the traditional nativity cave from late antiquity.
evidence.infer: Constantine/Helena’s Holy Land program (as in Eusebius).
evidence.debated: Exact Constantinian vs. later fabric in every wall.

items.connect_why: Egeria’s travel diary and Cyril’s Jerusalem preaching sit next to a church you can still enter.

items.name: Codex Sinaiticus (א)
items.date_note: Leaves now split among British Library, Leipzig, St Catherine’s, and the National Library of Russia.
items.found: St Catherine’s Monastery, Sinai (modern rediscovery 19th c.)
items.now: Primarily British Library (major portion); other leaves in Leipzig, Sinai, St Petersburg
items.line: The other great 4th-century Greek Bible, including the New Testament complete. A mountain monastery kept what empire-wide Christianity had come to treasure as Scripture.

evidence.shows: A mid-4th-century complete NT (+ OT portions) survives.
evidence.infer: Scribal collaboration, corrections, and early canon edges (extra books present).
evidence.debated: Production center; relationship to Constantine’s orders for fifty Bibles.

items.connect_why: Same story as Vaticanus: the Bible as a physical library object after persecution ends.

items.name: Codex Vaticanus (B)
items.date_note: One of the two great early pandect Bibles.
items.found: In Vatican Library by at least the 15th century (earlier provenance debated)
items.now: Vatican Apostolic Library (Vat. gr. 1209)
items.line: A nearly complete Greek Bible in neat parchment quires — the kind of monumental Christian book the fourth-century church could finally produce and preserve.

evidence.shows: A carefully corrected 4th-century Greek Bible survives intact.
evidence.infer: Links to Egyptian text-types and to imperial-era book culture.
evidence.debated: Exact place of production; relationship to Constantine’s Bible commissions.

items.connect_why: Athanasius’s canon list and Jerome’s biblical world meet an actual 4th-century Bible.

image.credit: Unknown source Unknown source ; file originally uploaded to the…

items.name: Dogmatic (Two Testaments) sarcophagus
items.date_note: From St Paul Outside the Walls context; now Vatican Museums.
items.found: Rome (associated with St Paul Outside the Walls)
items.now: Vatican Museums
items.line: A marble coffin crowded with scenes of creation, miracles, and Christ — theology carved in stone in the generation after Nicaea.

evidence.shows: Mid-4th-century Roman Christians commissioned dense biblical narrative sculpture.
evidence.infer: Visual teaching of creed-like themes (“dogmatic” nickname).
evidence.debated: Exact workshop date within the mid-4th century.

items.connect_why: Same decades as the Nicene settlement — belief you can run your hand across.

items.name: Gold glass: Christ crowning Peter and Paul
items.date_note: Met 11.91.4 Open Access.
items.now: Metropolitan Museum of Art
items.line: Christ hands martyr crowns to Peter and Paul. A toast to the apostles who Deep Dive readers meet in the earliest letters.

evidence.shows: Mid-4th-century Roman glass pictured Christ honoring the two apostles.
evidence.infer: Cult of Peter and Paul in Rome after the Constantinian peace.
evidence.debated: Cup vs. tomb-marker primary use.

items.connect_why: Same apostolic pair as 1 Clement — now in gold leaf.

image.alt: Gold glass: Christ crowning Peter and Paul

items.name: Gold-glass bowl base: Peter & Paul with christogram
items.date_note: Met 16.174.3; Open Access public domain.
items.found: Rome (typical of Roman catacomb gold glasses)
items.now: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
items.line: A sandwich of gold leaf in glass showing Peter and Paul beside Christ’s monogram — likely the base of a drinking cup later pressed into wet plaster on a tomb.

evidence.shows: Roman Christians pictured the two apostles with the christogram on luxury glass.
evidence.infer: Funerary reuse of feast vessels; devotion to Peter and Paul as twin pillars of Rome.
evidence.debated: Whether every piece began as a tomb gift or a household cup.

items.connect_why: Peter and Paul from the earliest Deep Dive letters, toasted on glass a few centuries later.

image.alt: Gold-glass bowl base: Peter & Paul with christogram

items.name: Hagia Sophia (Justinian)
items.date_note: Later mosque/museum/mosque history; still the great dome of Christian late antiquity.
items.now: Istanbul; standing building
items.line: Justinian’s Great Church — a dome that made pilgrims say the building seemed to hang from heaven. The architectural climax of the first Christian millennium.

evidence.shows: A 6th-century imperial cathedral of unprecedented scale was built and still stands.
evidence.infer: Liturgical and political meaning of the dome and nave.
evidence.debated: Details of original decoration lost or covered in later centuries.

items.connect_why: The empire’s church after the councils — and before iconoclasm’s fights over images.

items.name: Hinton St Mary mosaic (Christ roundel)
items.date_note: British Museum object 1965,0409.1; one of the earliest definite mosaic portraits of Christ in Britain.
items.now: British Museum, London
items.line: A floor mosaic with a clean-shaven Christ and chi-rho behind him — surprising, local, and intimate.

evidence.shows: A Romano-British floor featured Christ’s bust and the chi-rho.
evidence.infer: Christian ownership of the villa; possible catechetical or dining-room setting.
evidence.debated: Room function; whether Bellerophon panel on the same floor is Christian allegory.

items.connect_why: Chi-rho leaves the labarum and lands in a British dining floor.

items.name: Lullingstone villa Christian wall paintings
items.date_note: Roman villa in Britain with chi-rho and orantes.
items.now: English Heritage site; paintings conserved/displayed in connection with the villa
items.line: Orantes and chi-rho in a villa room in Roman Britain — Christianity at the far edge of the empire, in a family house.

evidence.shows: Late Roman Christians in Britain decorated a domestic cult room with clear Christian signs.
evidence.infer: House-church practice among villa elites.
evidence.debated: Exact liturgical use of the room.

items.connect_why: A reminder that the post-Constantinian church was also a household faith on the frontier.

items.name: Old St Peter’s (Constantinian basilica)
items.date_note: Replaced in the Renaissance by the present basilica; known from texts, drawings, and excavations.
items.now: Succeeded by the current St Peter’s; foundations and scavi remain
items.line: The emperor’s vast shrine-church over the memorial of Peter. It set the pattern for pilgrimage basilicas across the Christian empire.

evidence.shows: Constantine built a monumental basilica on the Vatican necropolis site.
evidence.infer: Liturgical layout, atriums, and relic focus of early pilgrimage.
evidence.debated: Exact construction phases and financing details.

items.connect_why: Eusebius’s Constantine and Egeria’s pilgrim world suddenly have a roof and a floor plan.

items.name: Pilgrim ampulla (Holy Land souvenir)
items.date: Early 7th century (Cleveland example); Monza collection earlier/related
items.date_note: Cleveland Museum of Art open-access example used for free image; Monza treasure is the classic Catholic reference set.
items.found: Eastern Mediterranean / Palestine production; collections in Monza, Cleveland, etc.
items.now: Cleveland Museum of Art 1999.46 (image CC0); comparable ampullae in Monza Cathedral Treasury
items.line: Tiny metal flasks pilgrims filled with oil from lamps at holy sites, stamped with crucifixion and other scenes — pocket-sized Holy Land.

evidence.shows: Devotional souvenirs circulated from Palestinian shrines in late antiquity.
evidence.infer: How ordinary pilgrims carried sacred contact home (cf. Egeria’s world).
evidence.debated: Exact shrine for each stamp type.

items.connect_why: Egeria describes pilgrims; ampullae are what they brought home.

items.name: San Vitale apse mosaic (Ravenna)
items.date_note: Justinianic Ravenna; UNESCO.
items.now: In situ
items.line: Christ enthroned in a glittering apse, with imperial panels of Justinian and Theodora nearby — theology and empire in glass cubes.

evidence.shows: 6th-century imperial Christianity sponsored complex mosaic programs in Italy.
evidence.infer: Political theology of Justinian’s rule in the West.
evidence.debated: Workshop origins and some portrait identities.

items.connect_why: The settled doctrinal empire after Chalcedon, visible in color.

items.name: Santa Sabina doors (crucifixion panel)
items.date_note: Among the earliest surviving public images of the crucifixion.
items.now: In situ on the church doors
items.line: Cypress doors with biblical panels, including a spare, early crucifixion: three figures on crosses, without later medieval agony style.

evidence.shows: Christians in papal Rome of the 420s could show the crucifixion on a church entrance.
evidence.infer: How late antique art approached the cross after centuries of reluctance.
evidence.debated: Whether every panel is original to the first installation.

items.connect_why: Same generation as Leo and the Christological debates — the cross now on the church door.

image.credit: The image of Jesus on the cross has been invented by commissioned…

items.name: Sarcophagus of Junius Bassus
items.date_note: Dated by the deceased’s epitaph; prefect of Rome, newly baptized.
items.now: Museum of St Peter’s / Treasury area (Vatican); casts elsewhere
items.line: Junius Bassus, a top Roman official, was baptized late in life and buried in a masterpiece of early Christian relief — Abraham, Daniel, Christ’s entry, and more.

evidence.shows: Elite Romans openly chose Christian burial art by 359.
evidence.infer: How classical style served new biblical subjects.
evidence.debated: Some panel identifications / program readings.

items.connect_why: A convert of rank, like the world Augustine later describes — carved in marble.

image.credit: No machine-readable author provided. Tetraktys assumed (based on…
